claims.claim: The page explains what each legislative stage is
claims.sourceSpan: A bill (or other item of business) may travel through a series of steps in the legislative process—from introduction to committee and floor consideration to possible presidential consideration.

claims.claim: The stages are sourced to the House rules, CRS and the Constitution, and the page also describes what a LegislationPatch bill card shows
claims.sourceSpan: This is a judgment call, not a statistical model.

claims.claim: CRS states that the process by which a bill becomes law is rarely predictable and for many bills will not follow the usual sequence of stages
claims.sourceSpan: the process by which a bill can become law is rarely predictable and can vary significantly from bill to bill. In fact, for many bills, the process will not follow the sequence of congressional stages that are often understood to make up the legislative process.

claims.claim: A House bill is introduced by electronic submission or by dropping it in the hopper, a wooden box on the House floor; a Senate bill is submitted to clerks on the Senate floor
claims.sourceSpan: In the House, a bill is introduced when it is submitted electronically or dropped in the hopper (a wooden box on the House floor).

claims.claim: In the Senate a bill is submitted to clerks on the Senate floor
claims.sourceSpan: In the Senate, the bill is submitted to clerks on the Senate floor.

claims.claim: On introduction a measure takes a designation based on its chamber of introduction, such as H.R. or H.J.Res.
claims.sourceSpan: Upon introduction, the bill will receive a designation based on the chamber of introduction, for example, H.R. or H.J.Res. for House-origi

claims.claim: A bill is typically referred to the committee or committees in its chamber with jurisdiction over its elements
claims.sourceSpan: it is typically referred to the committee (or committees) in that chamber with jurisdiction over its elements

claims.claim: On a multiple referral in the House one committee is designated the primary committee of jurisdiction
claims.sourceSpan: One of those committees will be designated the primary committee of jurisdiction and will likely take the lead on any action that may occur.

claims.claim: In the Senate, in almost all cases a bill is referred to only the committee with jurisdiction over the issue that predominates in it
claims.sourceSpan: in almost all cases, the bill is referred to only the committee with jurisdiction over the issue that predominates in the bill.

claims.claim: Each committee receives far more referrals than it can pursue, and the chair holds the chief agenda-setting authority
claims.sourceSpan: Each committee receives many bill referrals over the course of a Congress—far more than the panel is capable of pursuing in any detail. The committee's chair has the chief agenda-setting authority for the committ

claims.claim: Committees do not formally consider each referred bill
claims.sourceSpan: Committees do not formally consider each of these referred bills.

claims.claim: A discharge petition signed by a majority of the total membership of the House can bring a bill to the floor without the committee acting
claims.sourceSpan: The phrase ``a majority of the total membership of the House'' was construed to mean 218 Members

claims.claim: A bill need not be reported from committee before the House can consider it under suspension of the rules
claims.sourceSpan: There is no requirement that a bill must be reported from committee before the House can consider it under suspension.

claims.claim: A committee may hold hearings so members and the public can hear from selected parties about a bill
claims.sourceSpan: A committee may conduct hearings on a bill to provide committee members and the public an opportunity to hear from selected parties (e.g., a federal agency or organized interest) about the bill's strengths and weaknesses.

claims.claim: At a markup committee members vote on proposed amendments
claims.sourceSpan: it will hold a markup on the bill, at which committee members vote on any proposed amendments

claims.claim: A markup concludes when the committee agrees by majority vote to report the bill to its chamber
claims.sourceSpan: The markup concludes when the committee agrees, by majority vote, to report the bill (with any recommended changes adopted in the markup) to its chamber.

claims.claim: House majority party leaders generally decide which bills get floor consideration, either scheduling streamlined consideration or asking the Rules Committee for tailored parameters; Senate bills come up on a motion to proceed or by unanimous consent
claims.sourceSpan: In the House, majority party leaders generally decide which bills will receive floor consideration; typically, they schedule a bill for a type of streamlined floor consideration, or instead ask the Rules Committee to propose a set of tailored parameters for floor consideration. In the Senate, bills are brought to the floor only after the Senate agrees to a motion (typically offered by the majority leader) to proceed to a specific bill or, alternatively, if no Senator objects to a unanimous consent request to bring it up.

claims.claim: In the House most bills that receive consideration do so under suspension of the rules, which limits debate to 40 minutes, prohibits floor amendments and requires two-thirds of Members voting
claims.sourceSpan: In the House, most bills that receive consideration do so under a procedure called "suspension of the rules," which limits debate to 40 minutes and prohibits floor amendments, but requires two-thirds of Members voting to agree.

claims.claim: Other bills are considered under parameters set by a special rule reported by the House Rules Committee, which often operates as an arm of the majority party leadership
claims.sourceSpan: Most other bills are considered under tailored debate and amending parameters set by the terms of a special rule reported by the House Rules Committee (which often operates as an arm of the majority party leadership).

claims.claim: When a bill passes either House it is printed and that printed copy is called the engrossed bill
claims.sourceSpan: Every bill or joint resolution in each House of Congress shall, when such bill or resolution passes either House, be printed, and such printed copy shall be called the engrossed bill or resolution as the case may be.

claims.claim: The engrossed bill is signed by the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate and sent to the other House
claims.sourceSpan: Said engrossed bill or resolution shall be signed by the Clerk of the House or the Secretary of the Senate, and shall be sent to the other House

claims.claim: One chamber frequently agrees to the other chamber’s bill without changes, but sometimes proposes changes
claims.sourceSpan: One chamber frequently agrees to a bill—without changes—that was sent to it by the other, but sometimes a chamber proposes changes to a bill sent to it by the other.

claims.claim: Differences are resolved either by amendments between the houses or by an ad hoc conference committee producing a conference report
claims.sourceSpan: The chambers resolve their differences on the competing proposals either through a back-and-forth trading of alternative proposals (called amendments between the houses), or by convening an ad hoc conference committee in which Representatives and Senators from the relevant committees are appointed to hammer out a compromise called a conference report.

claims.claim: Amendments between the houses is also called amendment exchange or ping-pong
claims.sourceSpan: is called amendments between the houses (or amendment exchange, or sometimes simply ping-pong)

claims.claim: Once both chambers agree to the same text the bill is enrolled — prepared in its final official form and presented to the President
claims.sourceSpan: it is enrolled 51 —that is, prepared in its final official form and then presented to the President

claims.claim: The enrolled bill is signed by the presiding officers of both Houses and sent to the President
claims.sourceSpan: it shall be printed and shall then be called the enrolled bill, or joint resolution, as the case may be, and shall be signed by the presiding officers of both Houses and sent to the President of the United States

claims.claim: Enrolled bills are printed on parchment OR paper of suitable quality, as determined by the Joint Committee on Printing
claims.sourceSpan: Enrolled bills and resolutions of either House of Congress shall be printed on parchment or paper of suitable quality as shall be determined by the Joint Committee on Printing.

claims.claim: The 1990 waiver of sections 106 and 107 covers any reconciliation bill, appropriation bill or continuing resolution of that Congress
claims.sourceSpan: of any reconciliation bill, appropriation bill, or continuing resolution of the One Hundred First Congress

claims.claim: Successful overrides of presidential vetoes are rare
claims.sourceSpan: Successful overrides of presidential vetoes are rare, so Congress typically must accommodate the President's position earlier in the process.

claims.claim: If the President approves a bill he signs it; if not he returns it with his objections to the originating chamber
claims.sourceSpan: If he approve he shall sign it, but if not he shall return it, with his Objections to that House in which it shall have originated

claims.claim: A returned bill becomes law only if two thirds of each House agrees to pass it again
claims.sourceSpan: If after such Reconsideration two thirds of that House shall agree to pass the Bill, it shall be sent, together with the Objections, to the other House, by which it shall likewise be reconsidered, and if approved by two thirds of that House, it shall become a Law.

claims.claim: Override votes must be taken by yeas and nays with the names entered on each chamber’s Journal
claims.sourceSpan: in all such Cases the Votes of both Houses shall be determined by yeas and Nays, and the Names of the Persons voting for and against the Bill shall be entered on the Journal of each House respectively

claims.claim: A bill not returned within ten days, Sundays excepted, becomes law as if signed, unless Congress by their adjournment prevent its return, in which case it does not
claims.sourceSpan: If any Bill shall not be returned by the President within ten Days (Sundays excepted) after it shall have been presented to him, the Same shall be a Law, in like Manner as if he had signed it, unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law.

claims.claim: ROUND B FIX (material): the draft said two bills "have passed both chambers and are awaiting the President". A hostile pass found a third bill classified identically by the site’s own code — 119-HR-5334, stage "senate", step 3, likelihood 62 — and argued the count was wrong. Adjudicated in the main thread against data/cache.json: HR-5334 has NO House vote in votes[]; its own stored summary says the Senate REPLACED the House-passed text, so the chambers have not agreed on identical text and it is not awaiting the President. The count of two is right, but the sentence invited the challenge by asserting presentment the data does not record. Rewritten to state exactly what the data shows: two bills carry recorded passage votes in both chambers and are not signed.

claims.claim: ROUND C FIX (material precision): the draft said Congress "repeatedly passed provisions waiving the printed enrollment ALTOGETHER". Read in full, the 1 U.S.C. 106 notes do not support "altogether": each waiver drops the printing requirement before presentment and substitutes a HAND enrollment that a House committee certifies as true, and the provisions are captioned "SUBSEQUENT PREPARATION AND CERTIFICATION OF PRINTED ENROLLMENT" - the printed enrollment is prepared after enactment. Two hostile passes split on this (one called it accurate, one called it an overclaim); adjudicated in the main thread by reading the notes, and the overclaim reading is right. The sentence now says what the waiver substitutes and that the printing follows.

Both independently confirmed 119-HR-5334 is correctly excluded: three Senate-only votes, no House vote in votes[]. Round C also re-verified 30+ quoted passages verbatim and 36 ledger receipts; round D found no self-contradiction, no cross-page conflict with methodology.html, what-is-legislationpatch.html or how-we-track-voting.html, and no broken link or citation-list mismatch.

MAIN-THREAD CORRECTION to my own round-C fix: the replacement sentence first read "with the printed enrollment prepared afterwards", stated flatly of the whole waiver practice. Only a handful of the roughly dozen waiver provisions carry a subsequent-printing clause - Pub. L. 101-497, 101-466, 100-454, and the FY1988 provisions at Pub. L. 100-203 section 8004 and 100-202 section 101(n) - so a flat claim would have been the same over-generalisation the fix was correcting. After a hostile sign-off refused the sentence outright, it was rewritten again to anchor on the 1990 waiver, which carries the waiver, the certification and the subsequent printing in its own text. CORRECTION TO THIS NOTE: an earlier version named Pub. L. 104-54 and 102-260 among the subsequent-printing provisions; neither carries such a clause.
claims.sourceSpan: the Secretary of the Senate shall prepare a printed enrollment of the bill as in the case of a bill to which sections 106 and 107 of title 1, United States Code, apply.

claims.claim: SIGN-OFF FIX (material): the hostile sign-off DID NOT SIGN OFF on the rewritten waiver sentence, on two counts, both correct. The certification quote naming the Committee on House Administration comes from provisions that do not cover every class the sentence named (the sole debt-limit provision names the Committee on House Oversight, the same committee under its 1995-1998 name), and the subsequent-printing requirement appears in only about 5 of some 13 waiver provisions, so stating it of the practice generally was an over-generalisation. Rewritten to anchor on the 1990 waiver, Pub. L. 101-466, which carries all three elements in its own text, with the debt-limit class attributed separately to the 1995 waiver and the Code’s own note heading quoted for the run as a whole.
claims.sourceSpan: the Clerk of the House of Representatives shall prepare a printed enrollment of the bill or joint resolution as in the case of a bill or joint resolution to which sections 106 and 107 of title 1, United States Code, apply.

claims.claim: CROSS-BATCH ALIGNMENT (minor): the veto-cluster batch established that the reason usually given for a pocket veto being unoverridable rests on 1929 dicta. This article never made the override claim, but its gloss "turning on whether Congress is there to receive the bill back" stated the operative test as physical presence, which is the contested reading. Reworded to the constitutional test itself - whether the adjournment prevented the bill’s return. No new source needed; the clause is already receipted to the Constitution transcript.
claims.sourceSpan: unless the Congress by their Adjournment prevent its Return, in which Case it shall not be a Law

claims.claim: FINAL SIGN-OFF FIX (material, fourth pass over the same sentence, and the batch’s clearest lesson): the rewrite had read "The 1990 waiver shows the shape of it". Two independent hostile passes landed on the same objection - one graded it low, the sibling article’s pass REFUSED to sign off - and both were right. "Shows the shape of it" is a representativeness claim whose antecedent is the general practice, and it is not supported: only about five of the roughly dozen waiver provisions, all from 1987-1990, carry a subsequent-printed-enrollment clause, while the more numerous 1992-1999 group stops at the certified hand enrollment. Rewritten so every clause is attributed to a named, dated provision and nothing is claimed about the practice beyond "repeatedly waived both sections outright". The two October 1990 waivers are now disambiguated by date, and the 1995 provision’s own certifying committee is named rather than left to inherit the 1990 one.
claims.sourceSpan: shall be in such form as the Committee on House Oversight of the House of Representatives certifies to be a true enrollment.

claims.claim: FINAL CONFIRMATION ROUND (2026-08-31): a hostile Sonnet pass read the third rewrite of the enrollment-waiver passage in BOTH articles at once, having been told exactly why the two earlier versions were refused. Verdict: SIGN OFF on both. It confirmed every fragment verbatim, that all three elements attributed to the October 27, 1990 waiver really come from that one provision (Pub. L. 101-466), that the other October 1990 waiver is dated October 31 so the date disambiguates, that the November 20, 1995 waiver (Pub. L. 104-56) reaches a debt limit extension measure and names the Committee on House Oversight, that the U.S. Code note heading introduces the whole run rather than one entry, and - the crux - that no sentence now claims anything about the waiver practice as a whole beyond "repeatedly waived both sections outright". It also confirmed the two articles are word-for-word identical on the shared passage, so they cannot diverge in production. Two minor findings, both fixed after the pass and re-verified verbatim by a fresh source read in the main thread: "of that Congress" had no antecedent (the quotation now runs on to "of the One Hundred First Congress"), and this article had left a sourced frequency phrase unquoted where its sibling quoted it (now quoted in full). Both fixes are pure extensions of quotations the pass had already verified; they add no assertion.
claims.sourceSpan: any reconciliation bill, appropriation bill, or continuing resolution of the One Hundred First Congress

notes: First-refresh audit of a May 2026 pre-lane explainer, Phase B House-procedure batch. Two defects were disprovable against the site’s own data and its own audited pages: the claim that bills which have passed both chambers are shown at 100% (two such bills sit at 93% and 85%, and 2 of 68 signed bills are not at 100%), and the claim that a Rules Committee rule determines whether a bill can reach the House floor at all (CRS R42843 records that MOST bills that receive consideration reach the floor under suspension of the rules, and the site’s own suspension and discharge explainers document both rule-free routes). Two invented statistics were removed outright. The whole "what it means for passage" apparatus — odds language with no source anywhere — was replaced with what each completed step actually establishes. Round A (2026-08-31) was a fresh hostile Sonnet pass on receipts and figures: clean. Round B, a second pass on entailment and self-description, found one material defect the first pass could not see — the claim that two bills "have passed both chambers and are awaiting the President" asserted presentment the corpus does not record, and a third bill the code classifies identically made the count arguable. The count survived adjudication; the wording did not, and now states only what the data shows. Round B also completed the enrollment-waiver enumeration. Its four cross-page findings were artefacts of comparing against the not-yet-refreshed sibling page in the same batch. Rounds C and D then ran as two independent fresh hostile passes over the frozen draft. Both re-derived the live-data figures from cache.json and agreed with each other and with the main thread. Between them they found two more items, both fixed: the enrollment-waiver sentence claimed the printed enrollment was waived "altogether" when the statute substitutes a certified hand enrollment and has the printing follow, and the one frequency claim stated in our own words was replaced with the stronger wording CRS actually uses.
